sections.title: Executive investment summary: a niche engineering franchise priced for a growth rate it has never delivered

blocks.text: Triveni Turbine Limited (TTL) designs, manufactures and services industrial steam turbines up to 100 MW, and provides manufacturing, refurbishment, retrofit and lifecycle solutions for steam turbines and other rotating equipment up to 1,000 MW across multiple OEM platforms [F] (AR2026 p.4). It sells a customised, engineered-to-order capital good: management states that a 2 MW turbine and a 100 MW turbine are both customised, and that the company ships over 200 turbines a year [MC] (CALL Nov 2025). The business is run and reported as **a single operating segment - 'Power generating equipment and solutions'** [F] (AR2026 p.146); the product/aftermarket and domestic/export splits investors rely on are voluntary management disclosures, not audited segments.

blocks.caption: How FY26 revenue was actually earned (consolidated, Rs cr)

blocks.text: Mix: product sales were 72.5% of FY26 revenue (Rs 1,581.6 cr) and aftermarket 27.5% (Rs 599.5 cr, down 6.7% year on year); exports were 57.7% (Rs 1,258.1 cr, up 30.1%) and domestic 42.3% (Rs 923.0 cr, down 11.2%) [F] (AR2026 p.35). The audited geographic disaggregation is coarser: India Rs 921.7 cr, Europe Rs 554.3 cr, Rest of the world Rs 683.1 cr; the company states country-wise segmentation is impractical [F] (AR2026 p.146). Europe revenue rose from Rs 149.6 cr to Rs 554.3 cr in one year [F] (AR2026 p.146).

End markets disclosed are steel, cement, oil & gas, chemicals, sugar, textiles, pulp & paper, food processing, pharmaceuticals, geothermal, distilleries, refineries and fertilisers [F] (AR2026 p.26). **No revenue split by end industry is disclosed anywhere in the documents** - only the product/aftermarket and domestic/export cuts [AI]. Customers are EPCs, integrators, developers, IPPs and process industries; management notes the company sells to the integrator/EPC/developer and that permitting is the customer's problem, not TTL's [MC] (CALL May 2026).

Customer concentration flipped in FY26: one customer contributed 10% or more of group revenue, at Rs 349.8 cr (16.0% of revenue). In FY25 no customer reached 10% [F] (AR2026 p.146). The company does not disclose who it is, nor any top-5 or top-10 concentration.

subsections.title: Listing status and what it means for the evidence base

blocks.text: TTL is not a recent listing. It was a division of Triveni Engineering & Industries Ltd from the 1970s and was demerged into a separate listed entity with effect from October 2010 [F] (SCREENER); FY26 was its 31st annual report [F] (AR2026 p.37). The shares are listed on BSE and NSE [F] (AR2026 p.127). That gives us ten years of annual statements and twelve quarters of quarterly data [F] (NUMBERS), four full earnings-call transcripts, and a full annual report - a far better evidence base than an IPO-stage company.

The weakness is different: because there is no prospectus and only one reportable segment, several disclosures a buy-side analyst would want simply do not exist. **Not disclosed anywhere in these documents:** installed manufacturing capacity or utilisation; segment-level margins; revenue by end industry; customer names other than NTPC; top-5/top-10 customer concentration; the order-book to financial-statement reconciliation; a quantified peer comparison; enquiry-book figures on a quarterly basis (management explicitly declines these, saying they will be given half-yearly and annually) [F] (CALL Aug 2026). A credit-rating rationale was expected in our source set but the file retrieved is an ICRA subscriber log-in page containing no rating analysis [F] (RATING); the only rating facts we can use come from the annual report and the exchange filing [F] (AR2026 p.51; ANNOUNCEMENTS).

blocks.text: Classifying each driver: **structural** - 1 (aftermarket annuity), 4 (niche/technology barrier), 7 (installed base); **company-specific** - 2 (export build-out is a strategy the company executed), 3 (capital structure), 5 (US entry), 6 (new platforms); **cyclical** - 8 (order book tracks process-industry and power capex). The two drivers that matter most to the multiple, 1 and 4, are the two the documents evidence least precisely: the aftermarket claim rests on order intake rather than revenue, and the top-two ranking is a company statement citing a third-party database the report does not reproduce [AI].

subsections.title: Bear thesis: the strongest reasons not to own it

items: **1. Every scenario in our DCF sits far below the share price.** At Rs 568 the stock trades against modelled fair values of Rs 83 (bear), Rs 146.3 (base) and Rs 206.1 (bull) per share - implied downside of 85.4%, 74.2% and 63.7% [F] (NUMBERS). The reverse DCF says today's enterprise value requires about 58% annual sales growth for five years, against 15.2% in the base case [F] (NUMBERS).

**2. Ex the one low-margin turnkey project, FY26 revenue was flat.** Revenue rose Rs 175.3 cr; the new 'turbine extended-scope turnkey project' line contributed Rs 176.1 cr. Every other revenue line netted to minus Rs 0.8 cr [F] (AR2026 p.156). Management put that project at roughly a 3% PBT margin [MC] (CALL May 2026).

**3. Order booking went backwards in FY26 - and management had guided to growth.** Bookings were Rs 2,325.6 cr versus Rs 2,362.7 cr in FY25, a 1.6% decline [F] (AR2026 p.15), after management said in February 2026 'we are forecasting the company having a growth in order booking in FY 2026 compared to FY 2025' [MC] (CALL Feb 2026). Export bookings fell from Rs 1,258.5 cr to Rs 1,219.9 cr [F] (AR2026 p.15).

**4. The order book peaked three quarters ago.** Rs 2,220 cr at 30 Sep 2025 (+24% YoY) [F] (CALL Nov 2025), Rs 2,053.9 cr at 31 Mar 2026 [F] (AR2026 p.14), Rs 2,179.6 cr at 30 Jun 2026 [F] (PPT Aug 2026). The reported year-on-year growth rates (+8%, +5.1%) are true and the sequential direction from the peak is also true.

**5. Receivables have deteriorated faster than any other line.** Debtors turnover fell 9.54x (FY24) to 7.41x (FY25) to 4.35x (FY26) [F] (AR2026 p.15); our statements data shows 107 debtor days against a 48-day average over the prior three years and flags it red [F] (NUMBERS). The financial statements state the increase is 'due to increase in export sales and increase in credit period of the customer' [F] (AR2026 p.157). Receivables older than six months rose from Rs 61.2 cr to Rs 139.5 cr [F] (AR2026 p.138).

**6. Cash conversion has broken down.** CFO/PAT was 1.02x in FY24, 0.52x in FY25 and 0.32x in FY26; over three years cumulative CFO was 0.58x cumulative profit [F] (NUMBERS). Free cash flow fell to Rs 39 cr against Rs 349 cr of reported profit [F] (NUMBERS); on the company's own definition free cash flow fell from Rs 417.7 cr (FY22) to Rs 39.4 cr (FY26) [F] (AR2026 p.16).

**7. Margins are falling, and the headline margin flatters.** The company reports Q1 FY27 EBITDA margin of 18.0% against 25.8% [F] (PPT Aug 2026). That EBITDA includes other income; on our statements data, which excludes it, the operating margin was 12% against 20% a year earlier - the lowest in the twelve quarters we hold [F] (NUMBERS). Other income of Rs 28 cr was 40% of Q1 FY27 profit before tax [E] (NUMBERS).

**8. The addressable market is not growing.** The company's own market data shows the sub-100 MW steam turbine market excluding China and Japan at 7.0 GW in 2021 and 7.0 GW in 2025 - flat over five years - while the >100 MW market, where TTL does not sell new units, went from 20.5 GW to 53.0 GW [F] (AR2026 p.27; PPT Aug 2026). Almost all of the industry growth the presentation leads with is in a segment the company does not address.

**9. Foreign institutional holders have been leaving for six straight quarters.** FII holding fell from 28.34% (Dec 2024) to 20.58% (Jun 2026), a 7.76-point reduction; domestic institutions absorbed most of it, rising 10.63% to 15.99% [F] (NUMBERS). Promoter holding was unchanged at 55.84% throughout [F] (NUMBERS).

**10. Execution risk is now chronic, not episodic.** Four consecutive periods of disruption - the India-Pakistan conflict in Q1 FY26, US tariffs through FY26, the West Asia conflict in Q4 FY26, and 3-4x freight rates in Q1 FY27 [MC] (CALL May 2026, CALL Aug 2026). An analyst put this to management directly; the answer was that the only mitigation is a larger order book [MC] (CALL Aug 2026) - which is precisely what has not grown.

**11. Related-party purchases of scale from promoter-linked entities, with no stated substance.** Standalone purchases of Rs 73.96 cr from Triveni Engineering & Industries Ltd and Rs 36.86 cr from Subhadra Trade & Finance Ltd - the entity that holds 27.28% of TTL - in FY26 [F] (AR2026 p.111, p.100). Form AOC-2 discloses no material related-party contracts at all, every field marked 'NA' [F] (AR2026 p.54). The nature of the goods or services bought is not described.

**12. Promoter remuneration is large relative to profit and to peers of this size.** The two executive promoter directors drew Rs 18.87 cr in FY26 (Rs 11.50 cr to the Vice Chairman & MD, Rs 7.38 cr to the Chairman & MD) - 95.7x and 74.9x median employee pay respectively - against standalone PAT of Rs 336.7 cr [F] (AR2026 p.46, p.58, p.37). Total KMP compensation was Rs 26.51 cr [F] (AR2026 p.112).

subsections.title: Key debates: where the market may be wrong, in both directions

blocks.caption: Five debates that decide the outcome
rows: Is the order book a reliable forward indicator?
Rs 2,180 cr at Jun 2026, roughly a year of revenue, with management stating orders only enter the book once advances are received [MC] (CALL Feb 2026)

The order book is a management-defined, unaudited metric. The only audited backlog measure - Ind AS 115 unsatisfied performance obligations - is Rs 286.6 cr [F] (AR2026 p.158), because the standard counts only obligations against contract liabilities

Both numbers are correct and measure different things. The market treats a number that no auditor opines on as if it were audited [AI]. The Rs 286.6 cr figure is not the order book and should not be read as one
Is the receivables build timing or a credit concession?

Management says billing was skewed to end-March, that a significant amount was already liquidated by the May call, and that Q1 FY27 saw receivables fall and working capital revert to negative [MC] (CALL May 2026, CALL Aug 2026)

The audited notes say the rise was due to 'increase in credit period of the customer' [F] (AR2026 p.157), and receivables over six months more than doubled [F] (AR2026 p.138). Management also warned March 2027 receivables may be at a similar level [MC] (CALL May 2026)
Unreconciled. The two explanations are not mutually exclusive but the company has not quantified the split. Q2 FY27 receivables are the test
Is the aftermarket really the margin annuity?
Aftermarket order bookings +41%, share of bookings 26% to 38%, closing aftermarket book +115% [F] (AR2026 p.29; PPT Aug 2026)
Aftermarket revenue FELL 6.7% to Rs 599.5 cr in FY26 and its revenue share fell from 32.0% to 27.5%; spares revenue fell 10.7% [F] (AR2026 p.35, p.156). Margins by segment are never disclosed
The order-intake evidence is strong; the revenue and margin evidence does not yet exist. The bull case here is a forecast, not a fact [AI]
Is the US a business or an overhead?
Houston upgraded in FY26, positioned as both OEM and independent provider; management targets break-even in FY27 and profit from FY28 [MC] (CALL May 2026, CALL Aug 2026)

Triveni Turbines Americas Inc had FY26 turnover of Rs 64.3 cr, a loss of Rs 8.1 cr and accumulated negative reserves of Rs 34.8 cr [F] (AR2026 p.41). Management said Q1 FY27 carried 'a substantial loss' [MC] (CALL Aug 2026) and that US aftermarket has contributed less than 10% of the Rs 600 cr of recent aftermarket wins [MC] (CALL Aug 2026)
Currently an overhead with option value. The break-even claim is testable within two quarters
Is this a 20%+ compounder or a 10-15% compounder?
Three-year sales CAGR 20.5%, five-year 25.4% [F] (NUMBERS); management expects 'normalised growth rates' from FY28 [MC] (CALL Feb 2026)
Nine-year sales CAGR is 12.7% and nine-year PAT CAGR 12.2% [F] (NUMBERS). FY26 grew 8.7%; FY23-FY25 was a recovery from a depressed FY21 base of Rs 703 cr [F] (NUMBERS)
The five-year CAGR is flattered by a COVID-depressed base. The nine-year record is a low-teens compounder with excellent returns on capital [AI]

blocks.text: Our variant view is that the consensus debate is framed around the wrong question. The market argues about how fast TTL can grow; the more useful question is what the market is already paying for. At Rs 568 the shares carry 53.7x trailing earnings, 42.4x EV/EBITDA and 8.03x EV/sales [F] (NUMBERS) on a business whose nine-year sales CAGR is 12.7% [F] (NUMBERS), whose FY26 revenue growth was entirely attributable to one near-zero-margin project [F] (AR2026 p.156), whose order booking declined year on year [F] (AR2026 p.15), and whose addressable market by its own data has been flat in gigawatt terms for five years [F] (AR2026 p.27). The quality of the franchise - debt-free, 34% ROCE, genuine engineering barriers, an installed base that generates decades of service revenue - is real and not in dispute. The gap between that quality and this price is what the reverse DCF is measuring when it says the price requires roughly 58% annual growth for five years [F] (NUMBERS). The variant perception is therefore not that the business is bad; it is that a good business bought at a price requiring four times its historical growth rate is a bet on multiple persistence rather than on operating performance [AI].

subsections.title: What the timeline reveals about how recent the current business is

blocks.text: The engineering lineage is 58 years old; **the business investors are being asked to pay 53.7x earnings for is about five years old** [AI]. Every element of the current bull case is recent: exports crossed half of revenue only in FY26 (27% in FY22) [F] (AR2026 p.15); the Houston facility was incorporated in February 2024 and is still loss-making [F] (AR2026 p.41); full ownership of the African refurbishment platform was completed on 30 October 2025 and the legal merger only on 1 April 2026 [F] (AR2026 p.38); the aftermarket share of order booking rose from 21% in FY22 to 38% in FY26 [F] (AR2026 p.15); the CO2, ORC and MVR product lines have between zero and a handful of commercial orders each [F] (AR2026 p.29; CALL Feb 2026).

The corollary is that there is very little track record against which to test the new strategy. The US subsidiary has two years of accounts, both loss-making. The consolidated African platform has less than one year in its final form. The CO2 storage platform has one project, not yet commissioned, with management describing the technology validation date as 'a little premature for us to determine' [MC] (CALL Aug 2026). An investor buying the transformation story is buying management's execution record on the legacy Indian turbine business and extrapolating it onto four ventures none of which has yet produced a full profitable year [AI].

sections.title: The production chain: where value is created and where it is captured

items: **Step 1 - Qualification.** TTL must be pre-registered with consultants, EPCs and end-users before it can even be invited to quote. Management states the enquiry book only includes enquiries where the company is qualified, 'otherwise the enquiry would not be given to us by a customer' [MC] (CALL Aug 2026), and that it is qualified with all US consultants, OEs and EPCs [MC] (CALL Aug 2026) and with NTPC and major domestic EPCs for utility drive turbines [MC] (CALL Nov 2025). API Spec Q1, AS9100D and DGQA (Naval Warship Project) certifications are maintained [F] (AR2026 p.30).

**Step 2 - Enquiry and bid.** Conversion cycle is 6-12 months domestically and longer internationally; greenfield projects take longer than brownfield; some enquiries sit on the book for 18-24 months, others convert in three months [MC] (CALL Nov 2025, CALL Aug 2026). In the US, conversion is 'more than 12 months' [MC] (CALL Aug 2026).

**Step 3 - Pricing and order.** Contracts are fixed price. Management: 'We have a fixed price contract, so it is not a question of passing through price escalation ... these price escalations have to be absorbed at the point in time in the contract itself' [MC] (CALL Aug 2026). Bought-out content is locked with rate contracts or back-to-back orders at the time of bidding [MC] (CALL May 2026). Advances of 10-30% are customary [MC] (CALL Nov 2025); an order enters the reported order book only when the advance is received - the company lost roughly Rs 200 cr of Q3 FY26 bookings to this rule [MC] (CALL Feb 2026).

**Step 4 - Engineering.** Every unit is customised. R&D and engineering together are over 15% of the workforce (7.5% R&D, 8%+ engineering) [MC] (CALL May 2026); R&D spend was Rs 45.6 cr in FY26, 2.27% of standalone turnover [F] (AR2026 p.58).

**Step 5 - Procurement / balance-of-plant.** Bought-out content varies from 30% to 70% of an order and management explicitly declines to give an average [MC] (CALL Aug 2026). Subcontracting charges were Rs 71.5 cr in FY26, down 20% [F] (AR2026 p.35). 12.1% of input materials come from MSMEs [F] (AR2026 p.16), with Rs 112.6 cr owed to MSME suppliers at year end [F] (AR2026 p.117).

**Step 6 - Manufacture, assembly, test.** Explicitly not outsourced. Management: 'we think that areas such as quality, assembly, testing can never be outsourced ... you have to then be able to take the liability of that in front of your customer' [MC] (CALL Feb 2026). A fourth test bed with dynamometer power production was commissioned in Q2 FY26 [MC] (CALL Nov 2025); an in-house 15 MW load-test centre targets operational readiness in FY27 [F] (AR2026 p.32).

**Step 7 - Customer inspection.** A gating step outside the company's control. Deferred inspections pushed Q1 FY26 revenue into later quarters [MC] (CALL Nov 2025); management says inspection depends on 'customers' readiness to accept the turbine' [MC] (CALL Nov 2025).

**Step 8 - Dispatch.** Exports are shipped FOB - freight and logistics are the customer's cost [MC] (CALL Aug 2026). This is why a 3-4x rise in freight rates in Q1 FY27 caused customers to defer dispatches rather than raising TTL's costs [MC] (CALL Aug 2026).

**Step 9 - Erection and commissioning.** Rs 92.1 cr of FY26 revenue, recognised at a point in time [F] (AR2026 p.156). Management is explicit that it will add products 'without taking on sort of EPC responsibilities and the liabilities that come along with that' [MC] (CALL Aug 2026).

**Step 10 - Aftermarket over a 30-40 year asset life.** Spares (Rs 320.0 cr), servicing/O&M (Rs 251.7 cr) and REFURB, spanning turbines to 1,000 MW, gas turbines, compressors, blowers, alternator rotors and control systems from any OEM [F] (AR2026 p.156, p.8). Long-term service agreements are signed but only the portion executable within a year is booked into the order book [MC] (CALL May 2026).

subsections.title: Where value is captured, and capital intensity

blocks.text: Value is captured at two points. First, at the design stage, because efficiency and reliability are what the customer pays for: management says orders are not lost on price in the international market and that the proposition is uptime and robustness rather than being cheapest [MC] (CALL May 2026). Second, at the aftermarket stage, where the OEM is the natural provider and the customer's alternative is unplanned downtime. Everything in between - castings, forgings, balance-of-plant - is a pass-through where TTL carries the commodity risk on a fixed-price contract but earns no premium [AI]. That is the precise mechanism that compressed Q1 FY27 margins: orders taken a year earlier at then-prevailing prices, executed against bought-out costs that did not fall [MC] (CALL Aug 2026).

blocks.text: **Differentiated:** API-compliant oil & gas turbines, geothermal products, utility BFP drives, spares for the installed base, and the higher-value REFURB work (upgrades, reverse engineering, efficiency enhancement). These share three features - a qualification barrier, a customer whose downtime cost dwarfs the equipment price, and a design content TTL controls [AI]. The evidence is management's own pricing logic: the higher the specification, the higher the price per megawatt, with geothermal, BFP drive and API above process cogeneration at a sugar factory [MC] (CALL Feb 2026).

**Commodity-like:** standard process-cogeneration turbines for sugar, distillery and general industry in the domestic market, and the lower-value end of refurbishment (running maintenance, overhaul). Management is unusually candid here - domestic margins are structurally lower [MC] (CALL Nov 2025); orders are taken at whatever margin the market offers at that moment, and 'it is a competitive industry at the end of the day' [MC] (CALL Aug 2026). The balance-of-plant content, at 30-70% of an order, is pure pass-through carried at fixed price [MC] (CALL Aug 2026).

The uncomfortable arithmetic: the differentiated lines are, by the company's own disclosure, either small (spares fell to Rs 320 cr), early (geothermal, ORC, CESS) or below management's own expectation (API was 'lower than our anticipation' in FY26 and is targeted to return to only 10%+ of order booking) [F] (AR2026 p.156); [MC] (CALL May 2026). The commodity-like lines are where the volume is.

blocks.text: Under Ind AS 108 the group reports **one** business segment: 'Power generating equipment and solutions' [F] (AR2026 p.146). Consequently **no segment margins, segment assets or segment capital employed are disclosed for product versus aftermarket, or for domestic versus export** [F]. Every margin statement about these splits in this report is a management claim, not an audited figure. The company does disclose revenue by geographic region (India / Europe / Rest of the world) as required, and revenue by nature of product or service [F] (AR2026 p.146, p.156).

blocks.text: Source: [F] (AR2026 p.15, p.35); growth percentages [E] computed from those figures. **FY26 is the first year in this series in which aftermarket revenue declined**, and the decline (-6.7%) coincided with a 450 basis point fall in aftermarket's revenue share. Management attributes it to lower spares dispatches: aftermarket was 25% of Q4 FY26 sales against about 33% for the prior year, hurt by 'a lot of uncertainty' that depressed spares order booking, and by regional instability and travel restrictions in the Middle East deferring spares despatch and service engagements [MC] (CALL May 2026); [F] (AR2026 p.36).

**Our read [AI]:** the decline is real and matters more than management's framing allows. Spares is the highest-margin line in the business by management's own ranking [MC] (CALL May 2026); its 10.7% revenue decline in FY26 [F] (AR2026 p.156) is a direct contributor to the 160 basis point EBITDA margin fall the company attributes to 'adverse segment mix' [F] (AR2026 p.36). The bullish counter is that aftermarket order intake rose 41% and the closing aftermarket order book more than doubled [F] (AR2026 p.29, p.38) - meaning the revenue decline may be a one-year execution trough rather than a demand problem. That is a genuinely open question and it resolves in FY27 revenue, not FY27 order intake.

Management's explanation for the domestic decline is mechanical rather than strategic: 'our order booking in the domestic market was weak in FY 2025, and that is what is getting executed now' [MC] (CALL Nov 2025). The audited regional disaggregation corroborates the export story and adds a detail the management commentary does not emphasise - **Europe revenue rose from Rs 149.6 cr to Rs 554.3 cr while Rest of the world fell from Rs 805.9 cr to Rs 683.1 cr** [F] (AR2026 p.146). The export growth of FY26 was overwhelmingly a Europe event, not a broad-based one [AI].

Our read [AI]: this is partly strategy (a deliberate international expansion since FY22) and partly mix (a one-year domestic order trough working through). The FY27 setup is the reverse: domestic revenue grew 27.4% in Q1 FY27 while exports grew 10.8%, taking export share of revenue down [MC] (CALL Aug 2026) - and it is precisely that domestic-heavy mix which management blames for the 780 basis point Q1 margin fall [MC] (CALL Aug 2026). The 'export mix improves margins' thesis therefore cuts both ways, and investors should expect quarterly margin volatility to track the export share mechanically.

items: **Order-driven (long cycle):** the entire product business. Execution cycles are 7-8 months below 15 MW, 9-12 months for 15-45 MW, 14-15 months for 30-45 MW and roughly 18 months at 100 MW [MC] (CALL Aug 2026). Management is explicit that 'the execution in this quarter reflects the business environment and order intake of roughly a year ago' [MC] (CALL Aug 2026).

**Book-and-bill (short cycle):** spares, and part of service. Management describes relying on 'book and build of spares to come in, which has a shorter duration execution cycle' within the same year [MC] (CALL Aug 2026). This is the swing factor that determines whether FY27 growth lands at the top or bottom of the range.

**Genuinely recurring:** LTSA and AMC contracts, though only the next twelve months of each is taken into the order book [MC] (CALL May 2026), so the reported backlog understates contracted service revenue - one of the few places where the disclosure is conservative [AI].

**Project-shaped and lumpy:** the turnkey extended-scope work (NTPC CESS), refurbishment of large utility machines, and 100 MW-class product orders. Management: 'As we deliver larger and larger turbines and larger projects, the order booking will be lumpy' [MC] (CALL May 2026).

subsections.title: Is the export mix strategy or mix?

blocks.text: Both, and the documents let us separate them. The strategic component is clear and long-running: international hubs in Houston and Pretoria, service offices in London, Dubai and Indonesia, and 12 new customers onboarded in FY26 from Europe, the United States, the Middle East and Japan [F] (AR2026 p.7, p.31). The mix component is equally clear: the FY26 domestic revenue decline of 11.2% is the mechanical consequence of a weak FY25 domestic order book, by management's own explanation [MC] (CALL Nov 2025) - and it reverses in FY27, with domestic revenue up 27.4% in Q1 [MC] (CALL Aug 2026). Order booking tells the cleaner strategic story: export bookings went from Rs 467.8 cr (40% of the total) in FY22 to Rs 1,219.9 cr (52%) in FY26 [F] (AR2026 p.15). But even there, **export bookings declined 3.1% in FY26** [E] (AR2026 p.15) - the first decline in the series.

items: Principal exposures are US dollar and euro, with GBP, JPY, CHF and AED smaller [F] (AR2026 p.114). Policy is to remain 'substantially hedged through forward exchange contracts or other simple structures' [F] (AR2026 p.113).

At 31 March 2026 the standalone unhedged net receivable exposure was USD 7.29 mn (Rs 67.9 cr), EUR 10.54 mn (Rs 111.6 cr) and GBP 0.12 mn (Rs 1.5 cr) - roughly Rs 181 cr net long [F] (AR2026 p.114). Forwards outstanding to sell foreign currency were USD 21.55 mn, EUR 26.87 mn and GBP 0.19 mn [F] (AR2026 p.114).

The cash-flow hedge reserve was negative Rs 7.5 cr at year end against negative Rs 0.4 cr a year earlier [F] (AR2026 p.126), and Rs 9.45 cr of hedge losses passed through other comprehensive income in FY26 [F] (AR2026 p.125).

Management disclosed a mark-to-market loss of over Rs 8.5 cr in Q4 FY26 from rupee volatility and said such losses 'may be a recurring thing which happen every year because of currency volatility and our hedging policy' [MC] (CALL May 2026).

Management also claims currency depreciation is a margin tailwind rather than a competitive one, because 'we don't lose orders based on price in the international market' [MC] (CALL May 2026) - and pointed investors in Q1 FY27 to the gap between net income and other comprehensive income as an indicator of where margins are heading [MC] (CALL Aug 2026). That is an unusual way to signal forward margins and worth treating cautiously [AI].
Standalone foreign exchange earned was Rs 775.0 cr against outflows of Rs 181.3 cr in FY26 [F] (AR2026 p.58) - a large natural net long position that hedging, not netting, must manage.

blocks.text: The client roster that the documents reveal is genuinely high quality: a national generator, a national utility, a European large-rotor customer, a nuclear operator and a Middle East refinery. Each is a multi-decade asset owner for whom switching a qualified rotating-equipment supplier is expensive and slow. That is the substance behind the moat claim [AI].

Two qualifications. First, **not one of these relationships is quantified** - no revenue by customer, no contract values, no duration of framework agreements [F]. The case studies are marketing pages in an annual report, not disclosure. Second, the composition of the relationships has a common weakness: the Middle East API franchise, the SADC utility franchise and the US refurbishment franchise are each concentrated in regions that management itself described as depressed, small or slow during FY26 and Q1 FY27 [MC] (CALL Aug 2026, CALL Feb 2026). The stickiness is real; the growth within each account is not currently evidenced [AI].

TTL discloses an order book, and does so consistently every quarter - this is better than most companies of its size. What it does not do is reconcile that number to anything in the audited statements [AI]. That figure equals the contract-liability balance - it measures obligations against advances received, not the order book - and the Rs 2,053.9 cr order book is neither derived from it nor reconciled to it [AI].

Management's own words on what counts: an order enters the book only when the advance is received. In Q3 FY26 roughly Rs 200 cr of orders on hand could not be booked 'because those advances were not taken at the quarter end, and so therefore could not be accounted in our policy by which we record orders' [MC] (CALL Feb 2026). In Q2 FY26 management said 'We have finalised orders, but we have not taken them into our order book given the fact that we have currently not received advances' [MC] (CALL Nov 2025). This makes the disclosed number conservative in one direction and vulnerable to quarter-end timing in the other [AI].

subsections.title: Bottom line: is margin improvement structural?

blocks.text: **No - not on the evidence available.** Over the ten years in our statements data the operating margin excluding other income has moved within a band of 18% to 23%, starting at 23% in FY17 and ending at 21% in FY26 [F] (NUMBERS). The FY25 peak of 21.9% has already been given back. The one genuinely structural component we can isolate is employee-cost operating leverage, which fell from 15.1% to 9.9% of sales between FY22 and FY26 [F] (AR2026 p.16) - roughly 520 basis points of durable gain - but it has been fully offset by a rising cost of goods sold, from 55.2% to 56.4%, and by mix [E].

The bull case requires the aftermarket mix shift now visible in order intake (38% of bookings versus 26%) to show up in revenue mix, which it has not yet done - aftermarket revenue share actually fell from 32.0% to 27.5% in FY26 [F] (AR2026 p.15, p.35). Management's own standing commitment is deliberately framed at the PBT level and not the EBITDA level: 'a PBT margin of over 20% is something that we can maintain in the medium and long-term' [MC] (CALL Aug 2026). FY26 delivered 22.4% before exceptional items [F] (AR2026 p.36); Q1 FY27 delivered 15.7% [F] (PPT Aug 2026). That commitment is the correct scorecard and it is currently being missed [AI].

**Consequence:** any unit economics we construct are an estimate built on a management-stated unit count and a management-stated price band, neither of which is a disclosure. They are useful for sanity-checking orders of magnitude and for nothing else [AI].

blocks.text: The most useful output of this exercise is not the numbers but the shape: **TTL sells roughly 200 small machines averaging around 3 MW, at roughly Rs 6-7 cr each, with more than half the cost bought in.** That is a high-mix, low-volume engineering job shop with an annuity attached - not a volume manufacturer. It explains why physical capacity is not the constraint, why order-level margins vary 'quite drastically', and why a single Rs 176 cr turnkey project could swing an entire year's growth and margin [AI].

subsections.title: What would have to be true for unit economics to improve

items: **Higher megawatts per unit.** Management's explicit pricing logic is that higher-specification end uses command a higher price per megawatt: geothermal, boiler-feed-pump drives and API above process cogeneration at a sugar factory [MC] (CALL Feb 2026). The company already has orders in the 100 MW range and capability to 125 MW [MC] (CALL Feb 2026). Evidence to watch: API returning to 10%+ of bookings and revenue [MC] (CALL May 2026).

**Higher aftermarket attach per installed unit.** The single biggest lever, because spares carry the highest margin in the portfolio by management's own ranking [MC] (CALL May 2026). It requires aftermarket revenue - not just order intake - to grow faster than the product fleet.

**Lower bought-out share.** At 30-70% of order cost, every point of internalisation is margin. The company is doing the opposite of vertical integration, deliberately broadening its vendor base for flexibility [MC] (CALL Nov 2025), so this lever is unlikely to be pulled [AI].

**Overhead absorption at Houston and Pretoria.** Triveni Turbines Americas carried a Rs 8.1 cr loss on Rs 64.3 cr of turnover in FY26 [F] (AR2026 p.41); management targets break-even in FY27 and profitability from FY28 [MC] (CALL Aug 2026, CALL May 2026).

**Fewer strategic loss-leaders.** The single most controllable variable. A Rs 176 cr contract at roughly 3% PBT, on a revenue base of Rs 2,181 cr, costs the group roughly 150 basis points of blended PBT margin against a 20% portfolio average [E]. Management has said it wants more such orders [MC] (CALL Feb 2026), which is strategically defensible and margin-dilutive at the same time.

sections.title: Reading the statements like a forensic analyst

blocks.text: Our statements data is screener.in's consolidated series: ten annual periods plus a trailing twelve months, twelve quarters, ratios and shareholding [F] (NUMBERS). The annual report gives two years of audited consolidated and standalone statements and five years of company-presented key performance indicators [F] (AR2026 p.15, p.125). There is therefore **no audited ten-year series available to us**; the FY17-FY24 figures we quote come from the aggregator, not from audited statements we have seen. Where the two disagree, we show both and do not reconcile. The full statements are printed separately in this report; below we quote figures with years rather than repeating the tables.

items: **Growth has decelerated sharply.** Sales growth was 46.5% (FY23), 32.5% (FY24), 21.3% (FY25) and 8.7% (FY26) [E] on (NUMBERS). The trailing twelve months at Rs 2,252 cr is only 3.3% above FY26 [F] (NUMBERS). The nine-year sales CAGR is 12.7% and the nine-year PAT CAGR 12.2% [F] (NUMBERS) - the five-year figures of 25.4% and 27.9% are measured off the COVID-depressed FY21 base of Rs 703 cr.

**Profit has already stopped growing.** PAT fell from Rs 359 cr (FY25) to Rs 349 cr (FY26) and trailing twelve-month PAT is Rs 336 cr [F] (NUMBERS). Quarterly PAT year on year: -20.0%, 0.0%, -1.1%, +7.4%, -20.3% for the last five quarters [F] (NUMBERS). **Four of the last five quarters have shown flat or negative profit growth.**

**Other income is material and volatile.** Rs 76.5 cr in FY26, 12.9% of profit before tax [F] (NUMBERS; AR2026 p.36). It fell 5.5% on lower bank-deposit interest and mutual-fund returns in a falling rate environment [F] (AR2026 p.35). In Q1 FY27 it was Rs 28 cr against profit before tax of Rs 70 cr - **40% of pre-tax profit** [E] (NUMBERS). In FY22 it reached 62.2% of profit before tax because of the Rs 198.2 cr exceptional gain [F] (NUMBERS).

**Depreciation is rising faster than revenue**, from Rs 21 cr (FY24) to Rs 26 cr (FY25) to Rs 34 cr (FY26) [F] (NUMBERS) - consistent with the step-up in capex and right-of-use assets, and a mild forward drag.

**The tax rate is stable** at 25-27% across the period, with an effective rate of 26.1% in FY26 [F] (NUMBERS). The reconciliation shows Rs 4.25 cr of prior-year current tax adjustments relating to AY 2021-22 to 2025-26 and Rs 3.56 cr of prior-year deferred tax adjustments [F] (AR2026 p.146) - not large, but a recurring item worth watching.

**Exceptional items in two of the last five years.** A Rs 198.2 cr gain in FY22 and a Rs 15.7 cr charge in FY26 for new Labour Code employee-benefit obligations under Ind AS 19 [F] (AR2026 p.37). Standalone FY25 also carried a Rs 36.0 cr exceptional gain from the capital reduction of a wholly owned subsidiary [F] (AR2026 p.37).
**Total assets grew 23.7% to Rs 2,496.8 cr while revenue grew 8.7%** [E] on (AR2026 p.125). The entire gap is working capital and financial assets.
**Trade receivables rose 76.0% to Rs 639.1 cr** on 8.7% revenue growth [F] (AR2026 p.125). Gross receivables were Rs 677.0 cr against an allowance of Rs 38.0 cr [F] (AR2026 p.138).

**Other current assets rose from Rs 54.4 cr to Rs 209.7 cr**, a 285% increase, principally the unbilled portion of the turnkey project where revenue is recognised on percentage of completion with billing scheduled after year end [F] (AR2026 p.35). Contract assets due from customers on that project were Rs 99.9 cr [F] (AR2026 p.157).

**Trade payables rose 63.6% to Rs 558.1 cr**, of which Rs 102.1 cr is accrued project cost on the same turnkey project [F] (AR2026 p.35, p.125). Micro and small enterprise dues are Rs 112.6 cr [F] (AR2026 p.125).
**Inventories rose 25.4% to Rs 244.3 cr**, attributed to planned purchases for a higher order book [F] (AR2026 p.35). Inventory turnover nonetheless improved to 6.47x [F] (AR2026 p.15).

**The company is genuinely debt free.** No current or non-current borrowings on the consolidated balance sheet; the only financial liability of that character is Rs 35.9 cr of lease liabilities [F] (AR2026 p.125). Auditors confirm no term loans, no default, no wilful defaulter status [F] (AR2026 p.84-85).

**Liquidity is large.** Cash Rs 100.7 cr, other bank balances Rs 177.1 cr, current investments Rs 302.7 cr and bank deposits inside other financial assets of Rs 389.1 cr - the company's own aggregate of investments including cash is Rs 969.6 cr [F] (AR2026 p.125, p.139, p.16). Rs 99.9 cr was moved into deposits maturing beyond twelve months, which is why non-current other financial assets jumped from Rs 1.4 cr to Rs 101.7 cr [F] (AR2026 p.35).
**The current ratio fell from 2.22 to 1.98**, which the company attributes to lower cash and investment balances [F] (AR2026 p.36).

**Cash generated from operations fell 23.2% to Rs 238.1 cr and net operating cash flow fell 40.6% to Rs 111.0 cr** [F] (AR2026 p.126); income tax paid of Rs 127.2 cr consumed more than half of it [F] (AR2026 p.126).

**The working-capital drain is explicit in the cash-flow statement:** receivables minus Rs 313.4 cr, other assets minus Rs 160.3 cr, inventories minus Rs 50.7 cr, partly offset by payables plus Rs 269.3 cr and other liabilities plus Rs 23.7 cr [F] (AR2026 p.126). Net working-capital outflow of roughly Rs 231 cr against Rs 349 cr of profit [E].

**CFO/PAT of 0.32x in FY26 is the worst in the ten years we hold**, against 1.02x (FY24), 1.83x (FY21) and a three-year cumulative of 0.58x [F] (NUMBERS). This is one of the aggregator's amber-rated flags [F] (NUMBERS).

**Free cash flow collapsed to Rs 39 cr** from Rs 144 cr (FY25) and Rs 240 cr (FY24) [F] (NUMBERS). On the company's own presentation, free cash flow fell from Rs 417.7 cr (FY22) to Rs 39.4 cr (FY26) [F] (AR2026 p.16).

**Investing cash flow turned positive at plus Rs 21.9 cr**, because Rs 68.8 cr of mutual-fund redemptions and Rs 44.2 cr of interest received more than funded Rs 71.6 cr of capex [F] (AR2026 p.126). Liquidating investments to fund a working-capital year is exactly what a debt-free balance sheet is for, and the company had the room [AI].
**Dividends of Rs 135.1 cr exceeded free cash flow of Rs 39 cr** [F] (AR2026 p.127; NUMBERS). Funded from the investment portfolio. Sustainable for a year; not indefinitely [AI].

**Non-cash items worth noting:** Rs 26.3 cr of fair-value gains on current investments, Rs 38.4 cr of interest income, Rs 8.5 cr of credit balances written back and Rs 0.9 cr of share-based payment expense (down from Rs 2.6 cr) [F] (AR2026 p.126).

sections.title: Working capital: the single most important number in FY26

blocks.text: TTL's headline working-capital metric looks excellent and says almost nothing. The cash conversion cycle in our statements data is **15 days** in FY26 against 20 days in FY25 and 70 days in FY24 - an apparently continuing improvement [F] (NUMBERS). The company presents working capital excluding cash and investments of Rs 114.6 cr, roughly 19 days of sales [E] (AR2026 p.15). Both make FY26 look like a good working-capital year. It was the worst in a decade [AI].

The reason is that the cash conversion cycle nets receivables against payables, and TTL's payables ballooned in step with its receivables - trade payables rose 63.6% while receivables rose 76.0% [E] (AR2026 p.125). A cycle that improves because you are paying suppliers more slowly while customers pay you more slowly is not an improvement; it is a transfer of the strain down the supply chain [AI]. The cash-flow statement, which cannot be netted, tells the truth: operating cash flow fell 40.6% to Rs 111 cr on profit of Rs 349 cr [F] (AR2026 p.126; NUMBERS).

subsections.title: The two questions the scores cannot answer

items: **Does the moat convert into margin, or only into order retention?** Over the ten years in our statements data the operating margin excluding other income has moved between 18% and 23% with no trend, ending FY26 at 20.7% against 23% in FY17 [F] (NUMBERS). A genuine pricing moat should widen margins as the installed base and qualification set grow. It has not. Management's own framing supports order retention rather than price: 'we don't lose orders based on price ... all you could say that we may have the luxury of a higher margin' [MC] (CALL May 2026) - the luxury has not shown up in the numbers [AI].

**Does the aftermarket annuity survive TTL's own strategy?** Triveni REFURB explicitly services other manufacturers' rotating equipment - steam turbines to 1,000 MW, gas turbines, compressors, blowers, alternator rotors - of 'any make and any age' [F] (AR2026 p.8). That is TTL attacking other OEMs' installed bases. The obvious question, which no document addresses, is whether those OEMs and the independent service sector can and will do the same to TTL's 6,000 units, and whether the multi-OEM service market carries the same margin as captive spares. Management's ranking - spares highest, then aftermarket generally [MC] (CALL May 2026) - hints that it does not [AI].

blocks.text: TTL has a real and durable moat of a specific kind: **a qualification-and-knowledge moat that protects access and share, not price.** The evidence for it is concrete - 418 IPR filings, API/AS9100/DGQA/nuclear qualifications, a 6,000-unit installed base in 80+ countries, an independently measured Net Promoter Score rising across five survey cycles, and a customer roster that includes a national generator, a national utility, a European large-rotor customer and a nuclear operator [F] (AR2026 p.32, p.30, p.9, p.5).

What the evidence does not support is the conclusion investors usually draw from a moat of this description - that it produces expanding margins and compounding returns on capital. It has produced a stable, unexpanding operating margin, and returns on capital that have just fallen from 41% to 34% because working capital grew faster than profit [F] (NUMBERS). The board-level research note in this dashboard describes the aftermarket as 'a moat that compounds rather than erodes' [F] (BOARD); the FY26 evidence - aftermarket revenue down 6.7%, spares down 10.7% - does not yet show it compounding [F] (AR2026 p.35, p.156). That is the open question the next four quarters answer [AI].

blocks.text: The presentation leads with a global steam turbine market that grew from 60 GW to 116 GW at a 17.7% compound rate [F] (PPT Aug 2026). That statistic is true and almost entirely irrelevant to TTL, because the company sells new units only below 100 MW, and the sub-100 MW market excluding China and Japan was 7.0 GW in 2021 and 7.0 GW in 2025 [F] (AR2026 p.27). **All of the headline growth is in the above-100 MW segment, which went from 20.5 GW to 53.0 GW and where TTL does not sell new equipment** [F] (AR2026 p.27). The company's own data contains this distinction; the presentation's framing does not emphasise it [AI].

items: **Start with the order book, not the market.** Rs 2,179.6 cr at 30 June 2026, book-to-bill of 1.07x in FY26, and coverage of about 0.97x trailing revenue [F] (PPT Aug 2026); [E] (NUMBERS). That is roughly eleven months of visible work, which for execution cycles of 7-18 months is adequate and not more.

**Then the unit economics.** Roughly 200-plus turbines a year at a blended Rs 6.6 cr and an average size near 3 MW [E] on [MC] (CALL Nov 2025) and [F] (AR2026 p.156). Growth requires more units, bigger units or higher aftermarket attach - nothing else.

**Then the three levers, each independently observable each quarter:** product order booking (Rs 1,447 cr in FY26, down 16.9% [E] (AR2026 p.15)); aftermarket order booking (Rs 878 cr, up 41% [F] (AR2026 p.29)); and average realisation, proxied by the mix of API, geothermal and utility-drive work in which management says price per megawatt is higher [MC] (CALL Feb 2026).

**Then apply management's own ceilings.** The US will not exceed 20% of the order book 'at its maximum potential' [MC] (CALL Feb 2026); heat pumps and MVR 'will remain small' [MC] (CALL May 2026); CO2 storage is excluded from the enquiry book altogether [MC] (CALL May 2026). Once those are applied, the credible medium-term growth engine is the aftermarket plus API plus geothermal - not data centres and not energy storage [AI].

**Concentration:** management describes the global market as 'largely oligopolistic' and the Indian industrial segment as served mainly by Siemens and TTL [MC] (CALL May 2026, CALL Nov 2025). The sub-100 MW niche is characterised in the annual report as 'technically demanding' and 'traditionally dominated by large multinationals', with TTL claiming a top-two global position [MC] (AR2026 p.28). No participant is quantified [F].

**Channel:** direct sales to end users, EPC contractors, integrators and developers, supported by in-house teams and 'experienced agents', with service offices in London, Dubai, Indonesia and South Africa and eight offices in India [F] (AR2026 p.7, p.21, p.60). Contracting structure varies by customer - 'Sometimes they club the contracts and give it to the gas turbine lead only. Sometimes they break it up and give it to EPCs. Sometimes they order everything themselves' [MC] (CALL May 2026).

**The combined-cycle channel constraint:** roughly 50% of utility-scale gas turbine capacity is built as combined cycle, but only 20-30% of sub-100 MW installations convert, and roughly 80% of combined-cycle steam turbine scope goes to OEMs that supply their own steam turbine [MC] (CALL Feb 2026, CALL Nov 2025). This is management's own estimate and it is the tightest constraint on the data-centre narrative.

**Customer economics that sustain the industry:** cogeneration solutions reduce power costs by 14-15% compared with independent power producers while ensuring continuous supply [F] (AR2026 p.31); management adds that the competition for captive cogeneration is not grid power but the customer's cost of capital, so 'the higher the cost of capital, the more relevant our propositions become' [MC] (CALL Feb 2026). In FY25, 70% of TTL turbines had a renewable fuel source while 70% of customers were industrial [MC] (CALL Feb 2026) - i.e. the driver is energy efficiency economics, not green mandates.

blocks.text: **Earnings are real but their quality has fallen materially over two years.** On the tests that detect manufactured profit, TTL passes cleanly: no capitalised development costs, Rs 4.2 cr of goodwill with no impairment, a negligible share-based payment charge, a stable tax rate, no restatements, a clean CARO, an unmodified audit opinion, direct customer balance confirmations and testing of non-standard revenue journals by the auditors [F] (AR2026 p.121, p.157, p.84-86). There is no evidence of aggressive revenue recognition, and the new over-time turnkey contract is correctly identified as the key audit matter [F] (AR2026 p.121).

What has changed is cash backing and composition. FY26 profit of Rs 349 cr was 32% converted to operating cash [F] (NUMBERS), included Rs 76.5 cr of other income of which roughly a third was a non-cash mark-to-market gain [F] (AR2026 p.36, p.126), and benefited from a Rs 14.3 cr year-on-year reduction in the credit-loss charge taken while receivable ageing worsened [E] (AR2026 p.125, p.138). In the latest quarter, 40% of pre-tax profit came from treasury income [E] (NUMBERS). On our scoring this is **good accounting attached to deteriorating economics** - the opposite of the more dangerous combination, but not a reason to pay a premium multiple [AI].

Our DCF model is a five-year free-cash-flow-to-firm construction: EBITDA less tax on EBIT, less capital expenditure, less the change in net working capital; sales growth fades linearly from a starting rate to a year-five rate; a Gordon terminal value is added; and equity value is enterprise value less borrowings [F] (NUMBERS). It is a mechanical, rules-based model driven off the trailing twelve months, not a bottom-up build of TTL's order book. We interpret it below; we do not extend it, and every valuation figure in this report comes from it [AI].

subsections.title: Interpreting the DCF and its assumptions

items: **The discount rate does most of the work.** A 15.0% WACC on a company with nil debt, 95.6x interest cover, an [ICRA]AA+ long-term rating and Rs 969.6 cr of investments and cash [F] (NUMBERS; AR2026 p.51, p.16) is a high hurdle. It is built as a 7.0% risk-free rate plus a 1.15 beta on a 7.0% equity risk premium [F] (NUMBERS) - defensible for an Indian mid-cap industrial, but it is the assumption an investor should argue with first, and the sensitivity grid shows the argument is worth Rs 30 per share at the base case [F] (NUMBERS).
**The terminal value carries 71% of the base-case enterprise value** [E] (NUMBERS). The model is therefore a statement about the perpetuity, not about FY27-FY31.

**The margin assumption is neither aggressive nor conservative.** 21% for the base case sits between the FY26 actual of 20.7% and the FY25 actual of 21.9% on the same basis [E] (NUMBERS), and above the 12% just delivered in Q1 FY27 [F] (NUMBERS).

**Working capital at 26.3 days is the model's blind spot** given that FY26 debtor days were 107 against a prior three-year average of 48 [F] (NUMBERS), and management has said March 2027 receivables may be at a similar level [MC] (CALL May 2026).

**The model excludes all option value** - the US installed base, geothermal, ORC, CO2 storage, the aftermarket order-book doubling [F] (AR2026 p.29); [MC] (CALL May 2026). A five-year explicit DCF is structurally unable to price options that pay off in years six to fifteen, which is the strongest legitimate reason a market price can sit above a DCF for a long time [AI].
**No new valuation figure appears anywhere in this report.** Every fair value, projection, multiple and implied growth rate quoted is taken from our model as it stands [AI].

blocks.text: **The key forensic conclusion.** Today's price requires roughly 58% annual sales growth for five consecutive years - nearly double the fastest year in the company's recorded history, nearly three times the three-year CAGR, more than four and a half times the nine-year CAGR, and almost twice the starting growth of the model's own bull case [F] (NUMBERS; AR2026 p.15). To meet it, revenue would need to reach roughly nine times the current level by year five, on a business whose own market data shows its addressable sub-100 MW segment flat at 7.0 GW over the last five years [F] (AR2026 p.27), whose order booking declined in FY26, and whose last reported quarter grew profit at minus 20.3% [F] (NUMBERS).

The aggregator's own rule-based screen flags this as a red item: 'Today's price implies about 58% a year sales growth for five years, against 15% in the base case' [E] (NUMBERS). It is the second of two red flags, the other being receivables stretching [F] (NUMBERS).

A 58% implied growth rate is not a finding about the company; it is the arithmetic consequence of a specific model meeting a specific price, and there are five legitimate reasons that arithmetic overstates the gap [AI]:

items: **The discount rate is punitive for this balance sheet.** 15.0% applied to a company with nil debt, [ICRA]AA+ and A1+ ratings reaffirmed as recently as 18 September 2026, 95.6x interest cover and Rs 969.6 cr of investments and cash [F] (ANNOUNCEMENTS; NUMBERS; AR2026 p.16). The model's own stated capital structure - a 0.2 debt weight at a 7.5% post-tax cost of debt - implies 13.5%, at which the base value is Rs 176.1 rather than Rs 146.3 [F] (NUMBERS).

**The enterprise value is not net of cash.** The model explicitly does not net cash out because the data source cannot split it [F] (NUMBERS), while the company reports Rs 969.6 cr of investments including cash [F] (AR2026 p.16). A lower enterprise value requires less implied growth [AI].

**A five-year explicit DCF cannot value an installed-base annuity.** 6,000 units in 80+ countries running for decades, with spares, service and upgrade revenue that arrives in years six through thirty [MC] (AR2026 p.5); [MC] (CALL Feb 2026). The model captures that only through a 5.5% terminal growth rate, which is almost certainly too blunt an instrument for an aftermarket that grew its order book 115% in a year [F] (PPT Aug 2026).

**The model excludes every option.** The US market, geothermal, ORC, CO2 long-duration storage and the utility-drive segment are each at zero or near-zero revenue today and are therefore worth nothing in this model [F] (AR2026 p.41); [MC] (CALL May 2026). Markets routinely pay for such options, and occasionally they are right.

**The base is depressed.** The trailing twelve months includes a Q1 FY27 in which margin fell 780 basis points on export deferrals and a near-zero-margin strategic project [F] (PPT Aug 2026); [MC] (CALL Aug 2026). Starting a DCF from a trough understates the run rate [AI].

blocks.text: **Our resolution [AI]:** all five points are valid and, taken together, they might narrow the gap substantially - but they do not close it. Even the single most favourable cell in the entire sensitivity grid, at a 13.5% WACC and 6.5% terminal growth, gives Rs 194.0 per share [F] (NUMBERS), roughly two-thirds below the price [E]. An investor who believes the shares are reasonably valued is not disagreeing with one assumption in this model; they are asserting that the model's entire framework - a five-year explicit period at an equity-like discount rate - is the wrong way to value a compounding installed-base annuity. That is an intellectually respectable position. It is also an unfalsifiable one over any horizon shorter than a decade, and it should be held consciously rather than by default [AI].

items: **Q2 and H1 FY27 results, expected early-to-mid November 2026** (Q2 FY26 results were reported on 12 November 2025) [F] (CALL Nov 2025). items: **Receivables stretching.** Debtor days of 107 against a 48-day average over the prior three years [F] (NUMBERS). blocks.text: **Simple average: 5.2 out of 10** [E]. The shape of the distribution is the message: the business scores 8-9 on balance sheet and accounting quality, 7 on moat, and 1 on both valuation factors. **This is a good company scoring badly because of its price, not a bad company** [AI]. Strip out the two valuation factors and the average of the remaining thirteen is 5.8 [E] - a solid but not exceptional operating business with two genuine weak points, working capital and growth durability.

Triveni Turbine is a genuinely good engineering business. It occupies a niche - industrial steam turbines below 100 MW - that global majors serve thinly, protected by qualifications that take years to earn (API Spec Q1, AS9100D, DGQA, nuclear, NTPC and EPC vendor approvals) and by accumulated aerodynamic and rotor-dynamic know-how that cannot be purchased, evidenced by 418 IPR filings and validation partnerships with IISc, Stuttgart, Milano and Genoa [F] (AR2026 p.30, p.32). It has built a real export franchise, from 27% of revenue in FY22 to 58% in FY26 [F] (AR2026 p.15), and a real installed base - 6,000+ units, 16+ GW, 80+ countries - that generates spares, service and upgrade revenue for decades [MC] (AR2026 p.5, p.10).

It is debt free with Rs 969.6 cr of investments and cash, 95.6x interest cover, an [ICRA]AA+ rating reaffirmed as recently as 18 September 2026, Rs 17 cr of contingent liabilities, no guarantees, no off-balance-sheet vehicles, negligible goodwill and negligible ESOP dilution [F] (AR2026 p.16, p.156; NUMBERS; ANNOUNCEMENTS). Its accounting is clean by every test we can apply. Its returns on capital - 34-41% ROCE and 26-33% ROE over five years [F] (NUMBERS) - are the kind that, if sustained for a decade, make an expensive entry price forgivable. And its aftermarket order book more than doubled in the last year, which if it converts is precisely the annuity the multiple assumes [F] (PPT Aug 2026).

The case against is arithmetic before it is qualitative. At Rs 568 the shares trade at 53.7x trailing earnings that are falling, 42.4x EV/EBITDA and 12.5x book [F] (NUMBERS). Our model's bear, base and bull fair values are Rs 83.0, Rs 146.3 and Rs 206.1 - implied downside of 85.4%, 74.2% and 63.7% - and the reverse DCF says the price requires about 58% annual sales growth for five years against a nine-year actual of 12.7% [F] (NUMBERS).

The operating evidence does not currently support any acceleration. FY26 revenue grew 8.7%, and stripping out one near-zero-margin turnkey project it was flat [E] (AR2026 p.156). Order booking declined 1.6% after management forecast growth [F] (AR2026 p.15); [MC] (CALL Feb 2026). The order book peaked in September 2025. Aftermarket revenue fell 6.7% and spares 10.7% [F] (AR2026 p.35, p.156). Receivables rose 76% on 8.7% revenue growth, with an explicit note that customer credit periods were extended [F] (AR2026 p.157). Operating cash flow was 0.32x profit, the worst in a decade [F] (NUMBERS). Q1 FY27 profit fell 20.6% with 40% of pre-tax profit coming from treasury income [F] (PPT Aug 2026); [E] (NUMBERS). And the company's own market data shows its addressable sub-100 MW segment flat at 7.0 GW across five years, with all the industry growth in a segment where it does not sell new units [F] (AR2026 p.27).

items: **The compounding outcome.** The aftermarket order book converts to revenue, its share returns above 32%, API recovers to 10%-plus of bookings, geothermal and the US add a fifth to the order book by FY30, and margin expands toward the 23% the bull case assumes. Revenue reaches roughly Rs 6,000 cr by year five on the bull path [F] (NUMBERS). Even then the modelled per-share value is Rs 206.1 [F] (NUMBERS) - so this outcome justifies the business, not the price [AI].

**The grinding outcome, and the most likely on current evidence.** Growth settles in the low-to-mid teens, in line with the nine-year record of 12.7% [F] (NUMBERS); margin oscillates in the 19-22% band it has occupied for a decade; receivables normalise only partially; and the company compounds book value at 20%-plus while the multiple compresses. Shareholders earn the business return minus the de-rating [AI].

**The stall outcome.** The addressable market stays flat at 7.0 GW [F] (AR2026 p.27), domestic demand stays weak as it did through Q1 FY27 [MC] (CALL Aug 2026), export order finalisations keep slipping on geopolitics, and order booking declines for a second and third year. Revenue growth falls to the bear case's 8.2% fading to 5.0%, with margin at 17% [F] (NUMBERS).

**The optionality outcome, which the model cannot price.** CO2 long-duration storage validates at NTPC Kudgi, a second and third order follow, ORC opens the low-grade waste-heat market, and the Houston facility converts the US installed base into a refurbishment annuity. None of this is in any projection because none of it has revenue today [F] (AR2026 p.41); [MC] (CALL May 2026). It is real, it is unquantifiable from these documents, and it is the honest reason a disciplined investor might still hold the shares [AI].
**What all four have in common.** The business survives every one of them - debt free, cash rich, clean books, no dilution risk. **The variable is the multiple, not the solvency** [AI].

subsections.title: Where the price sits against the modelled values

blocks.text: **No rating and no price target is expressed in this report.** Stating where the price sits against the model is a matter of arithmetic, and the arithmetic is unambiguous: at Rs 568 the shares trade 6.8x the bear-case value of Rs 83.0, 3.9x the base-case value of Rs 146.3 and 2.8x the bull-case value of Rs 206.1 [E] (NUMBERS). No cell in the nine-cell sensitivity grid, spanning a WACC range of 13.5-16.5% and terminal growth of 4.5-6.5%, produces a value above Rs 194.0 [F] (NUMBERS). The reverse DCF frames the same gap from the other direction: the price requires roughly 58% annual sales growth for five years against a base-case 15.2% and a nine-year actual of 12.7% [F] (NUMBERS).

items: **About a third of the gap is methodological.** A 15% discount rate on a debt-free, AA+ rated business with 95.6x interest cover is punitive; the model's own stated capital structure implies 13.5%, which takes the base case to Rs 176.1 [F] (NUMBERS). Enterprise value is not net of the roughly Rs 970 cr of investments and cash the company reports [F] (AR2026 p.16; NUMBERS). And a five-year explicit period with a 5.5% terminal growth rate cannot capture a multi-decade installed-base annuity, nor any option value from the US, geothermal, ORC or CO2 platforms [AI].

**The remainder is the market's assessment of durability.** A 53.7x multiple on falling trailing earnings, and a 12.5x price-to-book on a 26% return on equity, is a statement that the market expects this return to persist for a very long time and the growth to reaccelerate [F] (NUMBERS). The FY26 and Q1 FY27 evidence does not currently support that: growth of 8.7% that was entirely one low-margin project, order booking down 1.6%, aftermarket revenue down 6.7%, cash conversion at 0.32x and profit down in four of the last five quarters [F] (AR2026 p.15, p.35, p.156; NUMBERS).

**What would close the gap from the company's side** is not a better quarter. It is two to three years of the aftermarket converting from order book to revenue, receivables normalising, and order booking resuming double-digit growth - all three of which are directly observable [AI].

blocks.text: Our research view, stated without a rating: **this is a high-quality, conservatively financed niche engineering business whose operating momentum deteriorated in FY26 and again in Q1 FY27, trading at a price that every scenario in our model values far below.** The company is not the problem; the disagreement is entirely about what the installed-base annuity and the unpriced optionality are worth beyond a five-year horizon. Investors should resolve that question consciously - and should use the November 2026 half-year balance sheet as the first hard test of whether the FY26 working-capital deterioration was timing or terms.

This is initial coverage. No prior edition of this report exists in the evidence folder, so there is no previous quarter's guidance tracker, risk assessment or thesis to test against. summary.one_line: Triveni Turbine is a debt-free, high-return niche engineering franchise with a genuine qualification-and-technology moat, but FY26 growth came entirely from one near-zero-margin turnkey project, order booking and cash conversion both went backwards, and at Rs 568 the shares sit 64% to 85% above every scenario in our DCF - a price that implies about 58% annual sales growth for five years against a nine-year actual of 12.7%.
bull_points: [F] The aftermarket order book more than doubled: closing aftermarket orders up 115.1% year on year to Rs 624 cr at 30 June 2026, taking the aftermarket to 29% of the total order book from 14%, with FY26 aftermarket order booking up 41% to Rs 878 cr (38% of intake versus 26%) and REFURB bookings up 107% (PPT Aug 2026; AR2026 p.29, p.38). If this converts to revenue it is the higher-margin annuity the multiple assumes.

[F] The export franchise is real and built: export revenue rose from Rs 226 cr (27% of sales) in FY22 to Rs 1,258 cr (58%) in FY26, with Europe alone going from Rs 150 cr to Rs 554 cr in a single year (AR2026 p.15, p.146). Export order booking was 68% of Q1 FY27 intake (PPT Aug 2026).

[F] Balance-sheet quality is exceptional: nil bank debt, 95.6x interest cover, Rs 969.6 cr of investments and cash, Rs 17.19 cr of contingent liabilities against Rs 1,446 cr of equity, no guarantees, no off-balance-sheet vehicles, negligible goodwill and 0.03% ESOP dilution, with [ICRA]AA+ and [ICRA]A1+ reaffirmed on 18 September 2026 (NUMBERS; AR2026 p.16, p.125, p.156; ANNOUNCEMENTS).

[F] The moat is evidenced, not asserted: 418 IPR filings concentrated in turbomachinery and CO2 power systems, API Spec Q1, AS9100D, DGQA and nuclear qualifications maintained, blade-path validation at a German university, partnerships with IISc, Stuttgart, Milano and Genoa, and an independently measured Net Promoter Score up 128% across 204 customers (AR2026 p.30, p.32, p.9).

[MC] Optionality the DCF prices at zero: North American enquiries up 'near 1,000%' to about 3 GW of an c.18 GW product enquiry book, US tariff on TTL's range cut from about 56% to 18%, first geothermal turbine-generator supply in Southeast Asia, and India's first 160 MWh CO2 long-duration storage system at NTPC Kudgi (CALL May 2026, CALL Feb 2026; AR2026 p.38, p.9).

[E] Excluding one project, FY26 revenue was flat. Revenue rose Rs 175.3 cr and the new turbine extended-scope turnkey line contributed Rs 176.1 cr; every other revenue line netted to minus Rs 0.8 cr (AR2026 p.156). Management priced that NTPC contract at roughly 3% PBT and called it 'negligible and near zero margins' (CALL May 2026, CALL Aug 2026).

[F] Order booking declined 1.6% in FY26 to Rs 2,325.6 cr after management explicitly forecast growth, export bookings fell 3.1%, and the closing order book peaked at Rs 2,220 cr in September 2025 versus Rs 2,179.6 cr in June 2026 (AR2026 p.15; CALL Feb 2026; CALL Nov 2025; PPT Aug 2026). [F] Working capital and cash conversion have broken down: debtors turnover fell from 9.54x (FY22) to 4.35x (FY26), debtor days are 107 against a 48-day prior three-year average, receivables older than six months rose 128%, the notes cite an 'increase in credit period of the customer', and CFO/PAT was 0.32x in FY26 (0.58x cumulative over three years) with free cash flow of Rs 39 cr against Rs 349 cr of profit (AR2026 p.15, p.138, p.157; NUMBERS). The sub-100 MW steam turbine market excluding China and Japan was 7.0 GW in 2021 and 7.0 GW in 2025 - all industry growth is in the above-100 MW segment where TTL does not sell new units (AR2026 p.27). Q1 FY27 EBITDA margin fell to 18.0% from 25.8% on the company's basis, and to 11.5% excluding other income, with 40% of pre-tax profit coming from treasury income (PPT Aug 2026; NUMBERS).
